TMD-20261014-212450-8770.text: The Strangers I Knew
Prologue

I have never travelled by myself anywhere, certainly not somewhere as far as Beanibazar. When you come from a sheltered family like mine, travelling with company is always a must, at least a pair of two. Yet, here I was, preparing to journey to my ancestral village. My
dada bari.
On my own. For the first time.

I shall admit, I was surprised when I first found out about the plan. My dad being the strict and protective man that he is would never let his daughter travel by herself. He never let any of my four elder sisters either, yet here I was. What has changed?

I stared at the back of my father’s head as he scrolled through his phone while reading different articles on our country’s situation. My father, Harun, has always been very good at hiding his emotions. True emotions to be exact. And by emotions, I mean, I have never seen him cry. Being the short-tempered man that he is, I have seen his fits of rage, and I have seen him smile. But the only time I heard about him genuinely being happy was when my eldest sisters, Sharmin and Shumin were born. Perhaps it was the excitement of having his first children, but the stories I heard of the man he was then resemble nothing to the man I know him as. Almost as if they are different people.

Not to forget, those were stories I heard from my mom, not him. My father has never been the talkative one with his children, let alone make idle conversations. True, he has always done his duties as a father, fed us, clothed us, educated us, raised us. Everything a father was meant to do. But I can’t remember the first or last time I had a decent conversation with him.
Kun shomoi baraoi bai?
(When will you leave?)” My mother asked from the kitchen, walking into the room and placing a cup of milk tea before my father without turning her attention to me, but I knew she was addressing me.
Ou baroi zaimu
. (Just in a bit.)” I replied, watching her gracefully roam around the room before perching like a docile bird across from my father.

She was… rather good at concealing her inner thoughts. She, Fathima, always had a smile on her face, but she did have her moments of rage if we were unruly. However, I could never tell what she really thought now and then, and it made me wonder if she ever thought at all. My mistake, she did think; about Ahmed. Her only son.
A lot.

Ahmed was my mothers greatest joy, just like Shireen, my third sister was father’s greatest pride. They may have felt the greatest when they had their first two children, but the favorites were their third and fourth- Ahmed and Shireen. As for my fourth sister Tarin and myself being the last, I wasn’t sure.
I didn’t know what they thought of me.
The baroi zao ekhon. Baade der oizibo.
(Then you better leave now, lest it becomes late.)” Were my father’s words to me, barely looking up from the phone in hand. But I could sense the concern edged in his voice.
I’m sure they loved me, but sometimes I can’t help but wonder if I was something they considered a gift, a choice, or a responsibility.
I pursed my lips before getting to my feet, smiling at them. “
Acha.
(Okay.)”
Because when you have a total of six children, the excitement of parenthood already disappears by the time the third or fourth child is born, let alone the sixth child.
Turning to look at my parents sitting across from one another, I knew exactly what they were.
The textbook versions of parents.
To be on Your Own

The journey to Beanibazar was definitely not an easy one, especially when one is traveling all the way from the city to the rural village. But I had to make it anyway. Starting from Shaporan I hailed an auto rickshaw that drove me till the bypass road, from where I then hailed yet another auto rickshaw that took me further inside only to drop me off at Gulapgonj. Every time I finished a trip, I found myself releasing a sigh of relief knowing that I was getting closer and closer without getting abducted or harassed. A girl can never be certain.

Yet, my journey was far from over, but close nonetheless. I was close to Narafing, and from here on, I could travel via manual rickshaw, which was the part I was looking forward to the most. Riding a rickshaw all by yourself with the wind brushing past your face as it speeds by was a welcoming thought, especially when it was the rural breeze of nature.
Kano zaitha?
(Where to?)” Asked the driver I had managed to hail. My reply was quick. “
Beanibazar sinoin ni?
(Do you know Beanibazar?)”
Beanibazar khe na sine?
(Who doesn’t know Beanibazar?)”
Right.
“Beanibazar, Ramdabazar,
Sondogram
?” My attempts at narrowing down my location was laughable. I was only saying names of places registered in my national ID at this point.
Khano, point o namba ni?
(Do you wish to be dropped on the main road?)”
Alright. Here goes nothing. “
Khan’s residence sinra ni?
(Do you know Khan’s residence?)”
Imagine my surprise when he said he does. This man was a god sent. I was finally saved from further embarrassment.
From then on, the ride was peaceful. The man took his sweet time riding towards my
dada bari
, while I leaned back and sighed in relief. I was indeed relieved, to the point I found myself feeling drowsy with leftover sleep.
This was not a wise idea, falling asleep in a rickshaw. But somehow, I found myself being lulled to a peaceful sleep, leaving my fate up to the heavens.

I don’t know for how long I slept, or if I had even slept to begin with. All I can say is I had just brushed my eyelids shut, maybe for a minute, or maybe a second, before I felt the rickshaw come to a stop.
Afa, utokka. Aicchi
. (Sister, wake up. We’re here.)”
Already?
My eyelids fluttered open, and true to his words, we had made it. I was right before the massive gates that led to my ancestral home, where my uncles and aunts were still there.
Only that something didn’t seem… right.
The gate seemed so… new. Like it was newly painted. Yet the paint was chipped, but the gate was in better condition than I had last seen it. And the place-
“Afa, bara dibani? (Sister, the fare?)”
Right. The fare- WOAH!
I almost flinched at the sight of the old man before me. Because up until a moment ago, it wasn’t an old man riding me.
Wasn’t it… a middle-aged man? Or did I get it wrong? Did I not look at his face enough?
But then… the rickshaw…
It was manual.
But I remember hailing a motor rickshaw.
What… is going on? Am I dreaming?
The Face of Unfamiliarity

Everything seemed to become a hazy mess before my eyes. I did not know how I paid the man and began making my way forward. All I knew was that my heart was in my throat, and my senses alert to the very strange and unfamiliar scent around me. Almost like it was… ancient.
Nothing felt familiar in this very familiar place. I remember there used to be a grocery shop outside the gates
Dola sasa
had made. Did they break it down? I don’t know. But the deeper I went, the stranger it got.
Because now I was finally seeing people around, people I call my family. But for some reason, most of them were… children. There were hardly any adults around.
The sound of laughter and giggles grew louder as I drew closer, making my way to a group of children playing on the mud. At the sight of me approaching them, their smiles faltered.
“H-Hi.” I greeted in English like the fool I was.
Silence.
Umm, ikta kita Khan residence ni?
(Is this Khan residence?)”
More silence. Until one of them turned to whisper something in another ear before they jumped to their feet and just like that, they took off. And all I could think was, did I say something wrong?

The kids were gone. Not just the kids I spoke to, but every other kid around as well. The whole place was vacant, like everyone had disappeared at the sight of me. I had no idea what was going on, or if there were any adults, but I needed to find answers. I needed to know where I was because this was certainly not my home. It looked like my home, but it wasn’t home.
“The renovations in
Boro sasa’s
house are gone. The study room
abbu
built in our house is gone too. In fact, the bedroom
abbu
built for
Moulana sasa

is gone too! And it was constructed two decades ago!” I stopped wherever I was going with a stomp of my foot, unable to believe what I had just seen. “How did everything disappear in less than a year!?”

And the more I think about it, the more it looks odd. I… could not recognize anyone. No matter how little I may have seen of them, I know who my relatives are! There is no way they all just disappeared into thin air and were replaced by children I never saw over there in my life!
So caught up in my train of thoughts, it takes me a while to realize I’m no longer in the Khan residence territory. I was somewhere else, like a rice field.
“Great. Now where the hell did I-”
Until I saw him. A young boy. In the rice field.

Sitting there all by himself, staring into the distance while being surrounded by cows and calves of all sizes. There he was, all alone in that massive watery field, with nothing but his cattle as company. And he looked so… peaceful.
Who are you? And why do you look so familiar?
I did not have long to dwell on it, because just then, my heart leaped out of my chest.
BANG!
The sound of gunfire.
I would be lying if I said I did not jump out of my skin when the shot was fired, followed by another, and another, until it was non stop.
“W-What… what is… what is going on… I-”
Words failed me, for fear had gripped me so hard I was rooted to my spot, unable to move. Tears burned my eyes making it harder to see, for I had no idea where I was, and now there were gunshots.
Could this day get any worse?
Just as I found myself resigning to my fate, I felt a tiny grip on my arm, yanking me towards them.
Ino ubai ruilai khene!? Lukao!
(Why are you just standing there!? Hide!)” It was the young boy from earlier.

I had no idea who he was, yet I found myself being dragged by him until we were both in the rice field, waist deep, before he sucked a breath and motioned for me to do the same. And like a child, I did as told.
And then, we dived in.
The Boy You Are

I don’t know how long we stayed under that murky water with rice plants all over us, but I knew one thing. The boy never let go of my hand. When we finally pulled up, the gunshots were gone. Like they never happened in the first place.
Was I imagining it? But the boy heard them too. Speaking of-

I coughed out whatever murk I may have swallowed, and so did the boy. But unlike my startled self, the boy looked entirely unfazed, like he was used to these things. But how come? This is the first time I’m hearing about a shootout in Beanibazar.
Dhuk faiso? (
Are you hurt?)”
I turned to the young boy looking up at me with his dark black eyes, unable to form any words. Because the more I looked at him, the familiar it got, until I was looking at someone else entirely.
A sudden gasp left my lips as I remembered something, looking at our surroundings. “
T-Thumar gai-
(Your cows-)”

But the boy only waved at me dismissively, something I noticed was an elderly gesture which this young man had learnt, before he whistled, and out came his herd from the water, having hidden just like us. Smart.
I smiled at the sight of the boy with his cows despite myself, until a thought struck me, my smile faltering immediately. This scene, I feel like I saw it somewhere. Or more like I heard it.
The boy that hid with his cows whenever there was a shootout.
The boy…
But that was impossible. What I was thinking. It was impossible. It couldn’t be.
I stared at the young boy smiling at his cows, the smile I had seen a handful of times, yet I could always recognize it.
Dorayona. Itha oe kunoshomoi.

(Don’t be afraid. This happens sometimes.)” I heard the boy say, confident in his words like it was not a big deal, or confident that he saved a life. But I could not bring myself to smile with him. For I found my heart shattering for this little boy.
He then went on to say, “
Thumar naam kitha? Harigeso?
(What’s your name? are you lost?)”
“J-J… Jerin.” I don’t know if I could tell him whether I was lost or not. But I needed to know something. But the boy was already talking, leading his cows out with him. “
Kuntha oitho nai. Amar loge ao. Amar babai thumare shahaijjo korba. Thain manshore shahaijjo dein.
(Don’t worry. Come with me. My dad will help you. He helps people like you.)”
The boy was already out and making his way towards the route I had come from, further registering my fears to be true. But I had to be sure.
So, I stopped the boy, finally ready to get some answers. “Chele, ami faurilaisi. E-Ekhon… kun bosor? (Boy, I have forgotten. W-What… year is it?)”
The boy looked at me judgmentally, but I couldn’t blame him. I really sounded like an idiot. But he answered nonetheless. And what he answered made my blood run cold.
Buligeso? Ekhon tho unnisho shottor
No…
“Forgotten it? It’s 1970.”
But if one bomb wasn’t enough. He dropped another.
Ar amar naam chele nai. Amar naam Harun.
“And my name is not boy. It’s Harun.”
The Man You Become

I ended up following the boy. Following… Harun. He promised me his father was very generous and would offer me shelter till I found my footing or even offer me a job. I didn’t argue. I already knew that.
I already knew what sort of man my grandfather was.
So Harun led me to his house, to… my
dada bari

. Where I had already come and found it awfully strange with unfamiliar faces. Only this time, there were more adult faces than children, and they gathered around Harun like he was lost. I mean he did survive a shootout.
After that, everything happened in a blur. Someone took the reins of the cows from him, and before he knew it he was surrounded by children around his age. Children I now recognize all too well.

My uncles and aunts. Boro sasa. Gura sasa. Dola sasa. Moulana sasa. Mejo fufu. Suto fufu. Mejo sasa. Suto sasa. All… young children. Boro fufu was the only one missing, perhaps because she was already married.

Then I saw dadi. My dadi, fit and well, rushing to her boy to see if he was unharmed. She was… pretty. I had never seen her like this. The only time I saw her alive was on her deathbed. And then she died.

Then came my dada. And he was… every bit the man I thought he was. Imposing and daring. He died before any of us were even born, but I’ve heard stories of him. And he lived up to every single one of them.
The one that did not live up to his stories was Harun himself. My father.
Perhaps it is because I’ve heard of him as a young man, but never a boy. But the boy before me was anything but the man I know.

He convinced his father I was lost and scared, and my dada agreed to house me as long as everyone knew I wasn’t… a threat. He didn’t need to tell me what he meant, for I already knew he meant the Razakar’s, but he didn't know that term since they weren’t a thing until the following year. But I do. And I know what role they play.
I was still reeling back from everything that was happening around me when I found myself in new garments, courtesy of my two aunts who were now around my age or lesser.

I had no idea what to do after that. I was stuck here, in a time far off than my own, and I didn’t even know if it was a dream or if I could ever go back. But I didn’t have much time to myself, for just then, I felt that tiny tug on my hand again, only to look down at young Harun smiling up at me.
“Obai ao! Ekhta dekhaitham!
(Come here! I want to show you something!)”
It wasn’t anything grand. Just a game him and his siblings were playing. Gulli danda.

He asked me if I knew how to play, to which I said no. He then went on to explain me the game in an excitement I had never seen in him, eyes lighting up with giddiness. The rest of them had gotten into some sort of quarrel, but my mejo sasa, the calmest of them all, turned to me and asked if I wanted to play, to which I denied again.
Oisethe! Ar khelaithai nani!?

(Enough! Are we not going to play anymore!?)” That was my suto fufu, the ever calm and cute lady that I remember her as. One yell from her and all her elder siblings were in formation, ready to start the game.

And my father lost in a matter of seconds. I found myself stifling a laughter as he came to slump down on the floor beside me, watching the rest of his siblings play. While he watched his siblings, I watched him, intrigued at the little boy before me.
There were a thousand questions in my head, a thousand things I wanted to tell him. But none of it would hold any weight, for this Harun had no idea who I was. I know him, but he does not know me.

And looking at him now as he is, I wondered to myself. If this is a side of him I had never gotten to see, a side he had hidden away from us so well, what more has he hidden from us to see? What more do we not know?
“H-Harun.?”
“Hmm?”
What do you want to be when you grow up? Should I ask him that? Or do you have any friends in Zakigonj? Do you ever wonder who you’ll marry? How many children will you have?
Thumar kuno asha ase ni?”
Do you have any dreams?
Harun did not have to think long. It was like he has been waiting for someone to ask him that, the answer in the tip of his tongue. “
Ase! Ami ekdin doctor bonmu!
(There is! I want to be a doctor someday!)”
Oh.
You… wanted to be a doctor.
But he wasn’t done yet. It seemed like my question had opened a dam I didn’t know had so much water to flow out, with his eyes glittering in excitement as if he was already living that life.
Ami bouth taka khomaimu. Boro bai o medical forra! Ami than lekan medical foriya ekhta boror doctor oimu!
(I will earn a lot of money! Big brother is studying medicine as well! I will study the same and become a reputable doctor!)”
That is true. Boro sasa indeed studied medicine. He also became a rural doctor.
Ar ami desh bidesh gurmu! Mojar mojar khani kaimu! Ice creamor lekan!
(I will roam around the world! And I will taste delicious food! Like ice cream!)”
I chuckled despite myself.
Er fore, ami abar goro aimu. Ar maizir lagi shundor shundor shari kinmu. Chok choki otha.
(And then, I will come home again. And I will buy my mother pretty pretty sarees. The glittery ones.)”
No longer was his voice brimming with excitement, but a sort of calm belief, that the future was already in his hands. That it’d definitely come true.
Only that it never does.
And it’s not because of whatever happens next year. I know for a fact that he survives it, so the war doesn’t change the shape of his future. Something else does.
Harun is still smiling, but I can no longer smile along. I can only watch the boy I will one day call my father.
Because very soon, survival becomes your bigger concern than dreams, and the dreams you once saw become a luxury, so you choose to do things that will keep you afloat.
The Harun of today, doesn’t survive very long.
The you of today, disappears with the passing of time.
The Womanly Girl

I had no idea of the style of my coming here, or how anything worked. Because just as I found myself getting comfortable in this world, this world had other plans for me. As it turns out, it wasn’t done yet.
Harun! Obai ao! Babai dakira!
(Harun! Come here! Your father is summoning you!)”
Harun didn’t wait around or excuse himself the moment his mother hollered for him. Before I could even slip a word out of my mouth, he was up and running, leaving my outstretched hand adrift.
“W-Wait-”
But in all honesty, what could I even tell him?
Harun was gone, and so was everything else in my surroundings. And the next time I blinked, I was on my feet, in yet another familiar but unfamiliar place.
A lot remained the same here, unlike my
dada bari.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”

A tiny little voice. So small I almost didn’t make it out through the thick thicket of trees. Dusk had already fallen, so it was a hassle making my way through the rickety pathway, leaves crunching under my feet as the pathway finally cleared, and before me was the house that had not aged a single day. Everything was still the same.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”
A part of me already knew why I was here, but the closer I drew, and the clearer the little voice got, I found my breath hitching, especially when the owner of the voice finally came to my view.
There, on the veranda of my
nana bari
, sat a little girl no more than three, playing around with her collection of wooden dolls, repeating the same lines over and over again.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”
Chubby and pudgy she was, with little pig tails on both sides of her head, cheeks flushed with giddy excitement over the two lines she had managed to learn.

I could not pinpoint the emotion that was brewing in me at the sight of her as I inched my way closer, until I was on my knees, earnestly looking at her delicate face that I had stared into my whole life, albeit older. The face of the woman she’d grow up to be.
“Bak bakum payra,
Mathay diye tayra,”
“Bou sajbe kal ki,”
I found myself whispering, watching as her little head turned to look at me, chocolate brown eyes staring with curiosity as I continued. “
Chorbe sonar palki.”

The woman that had helped me pack my bags during my first year at school, packed my lunch a thousand times over the years, was here right before me, unable to form a coherent sentence without anyone’s help.

Chocolate brown eyes collided with chocolate brown eyes, both filled with a tenderness that comes at certain ages. Mine was more on the sentimental side as I placed on a gentle smile, watching her doe like eyes scan my face.
Thumar naam kita?
(What’s your name?)” I found myself asking despite a part of me already knowing the answer. Yet, somehow, what the little girl before me said was not even on my mind.
“Shuela.”
Huh?
Isn’t it Fathima? Am I in the wrong pla-
Right.
Mother’s maiden name. The one her family remembered as. Shuela.
I chuckled despite myself, feeling the sudden bile rise up in my throat as if choking me with unwanted emotions.
My mother, like me, was a little girl too.
Ino Khe!?
(Who’s there!?)”
Thundered a voice, followed by countless footsteps. I flinched and moved away from the little girl, just as a woman rushed forward and pulled the girl into her arms, checking for injuries.
The man to whom the voice belonged glanced at his daughter and his wife who had grabbed her, before turning to me after making sure she was unharmed. “
Afne khe, ar khare thukaira ino?
(Who are you, and who are you looking for here?)”

Unlike my dada, my nana didn’t pretend he was alright with an intruder in his territory. Perhaps it was because my great grandfather himself was a Pakistani, so my dada was more open to housing strangers as a gesture of goodwill that he learnt from his father. The same couldn’t be told about my nana. And that was alright.
He was protecting his only child.
My mother, was loved too.
So what changed? What happened in your future that your family, this very family that protected you so much, turned away from you when you needed them the most?
Was it the birth of your sister? Or the children nana will have with his second wife? Did things as the eldest child change for you after that?
Or because you marry my father?
When do you lose this innocence?
Wake Up
Afa, utokka. Aichi.

I bowed my head in respect, clasping my hands in front of me before I began backtracking away from there. There was no point of saying anything to them. I was an intruder, and that alone was a red alert for them in that era. I should just leave.
So leave I did, but I was a fool to think it’d end there. Because now I could hear them throw chase.
Oi! Thuin khe!? Ino kita khorre!? Oi!
(Hey! Who are you!? What were you doing here!? Hey!)”
Afa, utokka. Aichi.
Shit.
I have to run away from here! I have to leave! I have to-
Afa, utokka. Aichi.
“Afa? Afa!”
I have to leave… I have to leave… I have to le-
Afa!
(Sister!)”

My eyes snapped open, a gasp escaping my lips as I finally felt air suck into my lungs like I had been deprived of it this whole time. My eyes fell on the man, the driver that was yelling for me to wake up.
The rickshaw driver. The middle-aged man. It was him this time.
Amra aicchi.
(We’ve arrived.)”
He was right. We did.
We have arrived at my
dada bari
In 2026 this time.
Epilogue

“Aicho ni? (You came?)” My mother’s voice was the first to greet me when I got back, but I said nothing, watching as she placed plates on the table for dinner while my father washed his hands to eat. It was him next. “Khaar goro khailai? (Whose house did you eat?)”
I replied to them after that. We ate, and they asked me mundane questions, and I replied. Like every other day. Only it no longer felt like every other day.
I look at my father, as if looking at him for the first time.
The boy who dreamt to be a doctor, to study medicine and then travel the world. To taste new things, and buy his mother pretty sarees.
Only that you never become one.

You never became a doctor, Harun. You never study medicine. You don’t travel the world, and you don’t really taste new things. And you see very less of your mother in the coming years before she passes away.

Fate had other plans for you, and it had nothing to do with the war that would follow the very next year after I saw you. You will grow up to become a bright young man, a pride of your mother and sisters. But not in the way you imagined.

You will travel to UAE because life in Bangladesh had nothing for you. But life in UAE ends up delivering more obstacles than you expected. Still, you fight through. You fight through, and you marry my mother. And you have us.
The dreams of the little boy from 1970 are pushed far back in the corner of your mind because keeping your new family thriving becomes your first priority. The sacrifice of a father.

I then turn to my mother. The girl who was once so loved and cherished by her parents, protected and sheltered. The girl who knew nothing beyond her pretty clothes and dolls and the rhymes sung to her. The ever-carefree child who grew up too fast.

Sooner than later you have a sister, and your parents will play favorites, until you are no longer the little girl who knew nothing beyond her pretty clothes and dolls and the rhymes sung to her. You become the shield that takes the blows for your siblings, the job of the eldest child. And over time, you experience as the shield child curves you into being the wife people expect you to be, a mother the generation deems a perfect fit.
And then you have us, and like father, we become your world. Like your siblings, we become the one in need of a shield. The sacrifice of a mother.
They all grew up too fast. The lines in their faces tell that story.
Somewhere along the way, youth left you behind, and we were born. We became your world, your priority. Being parents overrode the idea to be dreamers.
After all, you too, were just children with dreams, like us.

And perhaps it does not excuse the feeling of depravity of love that I felt as your child, or the reasons why you had favorites. It doesn’t explain why you could ask you other kids about their day and never mine until I was the last person left at home. Or why my presence in the house was always compared to that of my siblings. Never too much, never enough.
But it probably explains why you both are the way you both are.
You may not have fulfilled your childhood dreams, but you became the perfect parents.
So, now that I look at you, I know a little more.
The perfect mother and father. But not mom and dad.
And I guess, that is alright.
For there is no saying what future has in store for me too. If I too, will be expected to grow up fast. If I too, will be forced to push my dreams behind and become a responsible adult.
So, I guess, it is fine.
It is alright.
I know parts of you, and you know parts of me. But we can never know everything.
We are all strangers to one another somehow. Strangers that we know.
THE END

TMD-20261016-195424-1136.text: Freedom is a word spoken so often, yet so rarely felt. Of all the forms freedom could take, perhaps flying is the most beautiful—but only for birds. We envy the endless sky they call home, yet are they born knowing how to fly, or
do they fall before they learn to soar?

A bird with black feathers and a heart far too large for its tiny body, lived in a small forest and spent its days among trees, flowers, and butterflies together with its friends. In the quiet forest, storms come here and there, creating a lot of mess in its middle-class nest. The first storm came and took away the little bird's one and only toy. It stopped mourning its toy because of the company of its friends. But soon, it was thrown into a bottomless wall. The sound of its crying echoed inside the empty wall, but no one heard. It tried to flap its dark wings as hard as it could, taking one step closer to the surface only to be pulled three steps deeper inside. It took a long time for Hope to reach the surface, only to see that they were doing great.

Hope fell into darkness more than once. It climbed out each time with trembling wings, only to discover that the world above had continued without it. So Hope flew harder, learned faster, and carried its wounds beneath its feathers where no one ever thought to look beneath.

Every night, while the forest slept, Hope spoke to the lonely moon as though the sky were the only place willing to listen. And every dawn, before the first ray of sunlight touched the leaves, it would lift its wings toward a distant mountain that no other bird believed could ever be reached.

Almost—just almost—before Hope took off toward its dream, another sudden storm came, stole something far greater and took away its dearest. Its dearest vanished with the storm without a sound, making all Hope’s efforts in vain. Agony should have been the first thing to feel, but Hope chose to laugh.
Some losses make us cry.
Others leave us smiling, because tears are no longer enough.

Hope learned that long before it understood the meaning. For no reason, it trapped itself inside its nest and looked at the sky, the clouds, and the other birds every day while singing happily. Staring at the blue sky, Hope didn't realize when its favorite color became green.

Beyond the forest lay an endless field. At its farthest edge stood a mountain dressed in evergreen. Flowers bloomed upon its slopes through every season, and butterflies drifted through the wind as though the mountain itself were breathing. From Hope's nest, it looked impossibly far away, yet impossibility had never frightened it.

Every morning before the sun rose, Hope took flight. Across the endless field it flew, chasing the same distant peak. But there was one cruel rule to the journey; every time it rested, it had to begin again from the nest. Day after day, season after season, those tiny wings carried a dream far larger than themselves.
Then another storm came.
Hope sped up to avoid the rain. Little did it know that, in a storm, rain is not the frightening part—thunder is.
The sky spun.
The mountain vanished.
Feathers scattered into the wind.
Then—
Silence.
The frozen ground reached Hope long before it was ready.

The snow did not burn Hope. It swallowed the sound of the fall, as though the world wished to forget that it had ever fallen at all. White slowly surrendered to crimson, yet the pain did not come from the wound. It came from the silence.
Hope struggled to lift its wings, only to discover there were no feathers left to carry upon the sky.
Night settled over the field. Then came the sound of slow, measured footsteps from all the directions.
"What happened, my little bird?" A deep voice echoed through the empty field. "I thought you almost reached the top of the mountain, sweetie." The voice was deep, calm, and strangely gentle.
Fear may control the body, but curiosity can defeat it in a single blow.
Hope peeked toward the voice, a lone wolf approached through the snow, walking with a limp. With every step, a dark red trail stained the white beneath its paws.
"You are wounded," Hope said for the first time, leaving every other question unasked. “Oh, you noticed,” The wolf laughed softly. Hope nodded, forgetting the fear..
"So are you, sweetie."
It sat beside Hope as though they had known each other for years.
"How did you fall, sweetie?"
"I didn't notice the thunder."
"No wonder they call you a fool." The wolf chuckled.
Hope lowered its eyes.
"A fool?"
"Yes, sweetie. They call you that because you carry what they have long forgotten."
Hope remained silent.
The wolf smiled.
"Hope. Dreams. Courage."
After a long pause, Hope asked quietly,
"Did you once have them too?"
The wolf's laughter faded into the silent night.
"Yes, sweetie."
Its eyes wandered toward the moon.
"I simply failed to notice the trap. (A pause) Do you not love your nest, sweetie?" the wolf asked.
Hope looked toward the moon hanging above the sleeping forest.

"I do," it answered softly. "The forest is calm. It is warm. It has always been my home. But promises and dreams never allowed me to stay. Distant miles kept calling my name, teaching me to fly, to run, and to keep going, even when every part of me longed to hold on."
The wolf listened without interrupting.
"So... you are like me?" Hope asked.
The wolf smiled.

"The pack I belonged to never saw my worth. They believed every wolf must hunt. I never chased prey—I chased fear away. Every claw of fear hated me like I was a plague. That was enough for them to call me useless."
Hope tilted its head.
"Why didn't you live as your nature intended? Aren’t your claws one of those fears?"
"My nature?" The wolf chuckled. "Who decided that being born a wolf meant I had to hunt? Must I become what others expect simply because they named me before they knew me, sweetie?"
After a small pause...
"We are just... us. Living for what we choose to live for."
For the first time that night, Hope smiled.
"You are different."
"We are different," the wolf corrected gently. "We are simply ourselves."
The wind passed between them without a sound.

Night slowly surrendered to dawn. The moon faded beyond the mountains, spring knocked gently upon the world, and the pain of countless struggles sank deep into their bones, just as the melting snow disappeared into the grass. At the same time, they looked at their fading scars not as strangers, but as two souls who had survived the same loneliness in different forms.
As the first light of morning reached the field, Hope whispered,
"Who are we, if we cannot simply be ourselves?"
The wolf raised its eyes to the rising sun.
“ Who will we become when all these scars fade beneath the morning light?"
As uncertainty met the rising sun, would Resurgam become the beginning of their own stories?

এত পরিষ্কার, সোজাসাপ্টা একটি আদেশ! কী সহজেই বোঝা যাচ্ছে যে গুদামঘরে ঢুকতেই ওপরের তাকে একটি নিঃসঙ্গ কৌটা পাওয়া যাবে, যেটার মধ্যে ‘ইয়ে’ রাখা আছে। কী রাখা আছে, তা জানা নিষ্প্রয়োজন, কারণ কৌটো নিশ্চয়ই একটাই সেখানে। ঢুকেই প্রথম ঝলকে যা দেখলাম, তা হলো—কৌটা রাখা আছে আটটি!
“মা! কোন কৌটা?” আরও স্পষ্ট বিবরণের আশায় প্রশ্নটা করে বসলাম।
“কয়বার বলতে হয় তোকে! লাল ঢাকনা দেওয়া যেটায় ‘ইয়ে’ রাখা আছে।”
লাল ঢাকনা দেওয়া মোট কৌটা পেলাম চারটি। এবার? চারটিই কি নিয়ে যাব? নাকি আবার জিজ্ঞেস করব? কোনটা কম বিপজ্জনক হবে? একটু নিচু স্বরে জিজ্ঞেস করেই ফেললাম, “মা, বড়গুলোর একটা? না ছোট?”

জবাবে পেলাম ভয়ংকর নীরবতা। তারপর জোরেশোরে পা ফেলে মায়ের হেঁটে আসার শব্দ। বড় এক ঢোক গিলে করুণ মুখে দাঁড়িয়ে রইলাম। ঝড়ের গতিতে ঢুকে মা হ্যাঁচকা টানে নামিয়ে নিলেন সেই ‘ইয়ে’র কৌটা। তারপর আমার দিকে কটমট করে চেয়ে বললেন, “একটা ছোট কাজ বললাম, তাতেও যদি একটু সাহায্য পাই! ওই আমাকেই চুলা বন্ধ করে ঘুরে এসে নিতে হলো। যা, তুই সেজেগুজে ঘরে ঢুকে বসে থাক। কিছু করতে হবে না তোর!”
অতি ছোট এই বিষয় নিয়ে মায়ের এত কড়া ঝাড়ি, আর তার সঙ্গে তাঁকে সাহায্য করতে ব্যর্থ হওয়ার লজ্জা—দুইয়ে মিলে চোখ ঘোলাটে করে দিল। মনে পড়ে, গাল ফুলিয়ে ঘরে গিয়ে বসে ছিলাম, বাবা এসে ডাক না দেওয়া পর্যন্ত।
আজ এত কাল পরও এই কৌতুকাবহ মীম দেখে পুরোনো এমন কত ঘটনা মনে করে একাই কিছুক্ষণ হাসলাম। মায়েদের বোধ হয় এটা এক প্রথাগত স্বভাব, নইলে পৃথিবীর এত মায়ের সঙ্গে আমার মায়ের মিল কীভাবে বের হলো?

মোবাইলফোনটি বিশ্রামে রেখে ঢুকলাম রান্নাঘরে। খালা মাছটা সুন্দর করে ধুয়ে রেখেছে। কষিয়ে একটু পানি দিয়ে নেড়ে নিলাম। অফিসের কিছু জরুরি ইমেল আছে, সেগুলো একটু দেখে নিতে পারি এই ফাঁকে—এই ভেবে রান্নাঘর থেকে বের হতে হতে বললাম, “খালা, দু-এক মিনিট পর মাছটাতে একটু ‘ইয়ে’ দিয়ে চুলার জ্বাল নিভিয়ে দিয়ো!”
পেছন থেকে অতি বিভ্রান্ত এক মহিলার প্রশ্ন এল, “আম্মা, কী দিমু?”
“উফ! ‘ইয়ে’ যে রাখা আছে, ওই বাটিতে—ওইটা ওপর থেকে ছিটিয়ে দিয়ো!”
“আম্মা! কী কইলেন? কুনটা ছিটামু?”
“ধুর খালা, সব তোমাকে এইভাবে ভেঙে বলতে হয় কেন? লাগবে না, যাও! আমিই করছি!”
নিজেই কুচি করে রাখা ধনেপাতা মাছের ওপর ছড়িয়ে দিয়ে চুলার জ্বাল নিভিয়ে বেরিয়ে এলাম। এত সহজভাবে বলা কথাও কীভাবে বোঝে না মানুষ, অবাক লাগে!
রুমে ঢুকতেই ফোন বেজে উঠল। নিশ্চয়ই মা।
“হুম মা, বলো।”
“কিরে, রান্না করিস? নাকি ছুটির দিন, তাই বের হচ্ছিস কোথাও?”
“না মা, রান্না শেষ। অফিসের কিছু টুকটাক কাজ আছে, সারব এখন।”
“আচ্ছা, কর তাহলে। তোর বাবার ‘ইয়ে’টা একটু পাঠিয়ে দিস।”
“বাবার কী?”
“উফ! ‘ইয়ে’টা নিলি না সেই দিন? তোর কাজ হয়ে গেলে দিয়ে দিস। তোর বাবা আজ বলছিল, তার লাগবে।”
দীর্ঘশ্বাসটা চেপে গেলাম। “ঠিক আছে মা, পাঠিয়ে দেব।”
ফোন রেখে বাবাকে একটি মেসেজ পাঠালাম, “তোমার কোনো জরুরি জিনিস কি আমার কাছে আছে, যা তোমার এখনই ফেরত লাগবে?”
বাবার উত্তর, “ওজন মাপার যন্ত্রটা। কাজ ফুরালে পাঠিয়ে দিস।”
চেপে রাখা দীর্ঘশ্বাসটি সুযোগ বুঝে এবার বেরিয়ে পড়ল। যাই, ‘ইয়ে’টা একটা ব্যাগে ভরে রাখি। বিকেলে পাঠিয়ে দেব। মায়ের কাছ থেকে আর কোনো রকম তাগিদ আসার আগেই।

বয়স হয়তো বেড়েছে ভালোই, চুলেও পাক ধরল বলে, তাই বলে মায়ের ঝাড়ি হজম করার মতো শক্তি এখনও আয়ত্তে আনা সম্ভব হয়নি। কেন যে মানুষটা একটু সহজভাবে বুঝিয়ে বলতে পারে না! ঠিকঠাকভাবে বললে তো তাঁর জীবনটাও সহজ হয়, সঙ্গে আমাদেরটাও। কে যে বোঝাবে তাঁকে!
আমি বাবা কখনোই এমন হব না। এইসব আজগুবি প্রথা আমি ভাঙবই, ভাঙব!

Baba’s Silence
Hama amada hastand?

(Is everyone ready?)” Baba’s voice echoed inside our silent house, his eyes never meeting ours as we nodded, before he began walking out with the rest of us following behind like ducklings following their mother duck.

Our little journey to the cars awaiting us outside was eerily silent, with just the sound of our burkas swishing with the movement of our legs while I clasped my gloved hands in front of me. My sisters, their husbands, and my brother held equal expressions before we finally made it to the cars that will take us to our ancestral home in Istalif.

Baba was on the front seat with the driver, with Jawad, my brother, my third and fourth sister, Laila and Nilab, and I on the back, our emotions shrouded behind our niqabs. In the second car was my eldest sister Marzia, her husband Hamid and my second sister Soraya, with her husband Farid. Hamid and Farid never really got along, so I cannot say how awkward that ride must have been. I mean, my own ride was awkward enough, with not a single word exchanged. Or was it a peaceful silence in disguise?
There was a third vehicle trailing behind us, silently, all alone, but a part of us nonetheless. Nobody inside my car spoke a word about it.

The city of Kabul passed by us in the blink of an eye, until we were surrounded by lush greenery, followed by mountainous terrains. Not long after that, the roads began to look familiar, livelier, as villages came to view and I knew we had made it to Istalif. And soon, we’d make it to our ancestral home, where I’d finally have to face my reality. The reality I’m trying so hard to avoid.

Someone in the car sniffled, I couldn’t say who, and I didn’t want to find out either. Comforting each other was pointless, for there was no comfort to be found anywhere at the moment. Speaking would only make me confront the reality, and the reality would make me do more than just sniffle, and I didn’t want to do that just yet. For the little time I have been given to myself, I wish to spend it in quietness, without thinking about where I’m headed.

At long last, the cars came to a stop, but not without being greeted by a series of faces of men I quickly recognized as my uncles and cousin brothers, all holding solemn expressions as they made way for me and my sisters to be let out.

Like a puppet, I followed my sisters’ movements and went wherever they did, but I could not bring myself to lift my head and look up at whatever everyone else was looking as the third vehicle rounded the corner and came to a stop before everyone’s eyes, and there it was. The bier.

The sniffles got louder among the ladies, but quiet enough not to anger the men as they all gathered around the bier to lift it up and place it inside our house, where my maman will receive her final goodbyes from the family she had known for more than fifty years.

Yet, I could not bring myself to lift my head, even as my maman, now wrapped inside a kafan and held up by the bier, was placed in her living room that she had decorated herself years ago. As the scent of incense took over the whole area and people began excusing themselves to give us, her children and husband, a minute.
Yet, I could not lift my head.
I could not, for the life of me, still accept that maman, whose warm hands I held not even twenty-four hours ago, was now cold as ice. I did not even want to think of it.
I did not want to believe maman could die.
Why Maman?

Ever since my family moved back to Afghanistan from the UAE, there has not been a single winter in our lives when we didn’t have to visit the hospital. It was always one thing or the other, and it always concerned maman.

Starting from the winter of 2013, when she had her first brain stroke, not to forget the menopause and the toll it took on her already depraved health. Barely conscious, paralyzed, and sanity halfway gone, I believe part of her had already died back then.

The following winter was spent making sure we didn’t have a repeat of the previous one. Then came 2015, and we must have cut some slack, because then started her seizures, body convulsing like a fish out of water. It was scary, as if she was possessed, with her mouth foaming and eyes rolling backwards. The doctors later said she had epilepsy. Another added to the list.

There was no time to take precaution for the winter of 2016, for a surprise was already awaiting us. Maman was maman alright, but her body had started a new dance of trembling from head to toe- literally. Her speech was more disoriented, and she could barely hold an object without including it in her dance moves. We were later told she had Parkinson's.

Did peace return to us after that? Probably, if one can call it that. With the threat of dementia slowly taking over our maman day by day, we spent the next few winters in a strange bliss, ignorant bliss, perhaps. Marzia got married in the winter of 2018, which might have been the happiest winter we’ve had since coming back to Afghanistan. Then came 2020. Covid.

Not to worry, maman did not get diagnosed with that. We made sure she was protected to the best of our abilities. But unfortunately for us, we forgot to protect her from the rest of the demons lurking in the shadows.

When we rushed her to the hospital this time, we were told she had only three days left to live. Fifteen days for the GBS to take over the organs and shut them down, and it was day twelve already. Her whole body was paralyzed. The only thing functioning was her heart and head.
Lucky for us there was a cure, and it could still be administered before the fifteen days are up. It sure cost us a fortune, but we were willing to take our chances, no matter how slim it may be.
Maman, once again, beat the odds and survived. Recovery took months, almost a year, but she was alive and living, that was all that mattered.

2022 came and Soraya got married. This wedding wasn’t very fun, for like every winter, it was spent worrying over mothers declining health, and this time she could not make it to her daughter’s wedding even.

2023, and she was looking so much better than ever before, to the point she made a grand entrance to Laila’s wedding. It seemed like good fortune was smiling down at us in those years, for she was well enough to see through not only Nilab’s wedding as well, but also her first grandchild, Marzia’s daughter.
The heavens were really smiling down at us, only to hide their evil smirk behind.
Because it so happened that Nilab was the only one who didn’t marry during winter, so the winter of 2025 was still to be accounted for. And when it did arrive, it came bearing gifts.
Not only was maman diagnosed with severe pneumonia with risk of damaged lungs, but was also septic from the hospital ICU. Chances of survival were slim.
Fate is a funny thing. How it always expected maman to withstand all of this was beyond me. Maman was no wonder woman, how much more did they expect from her? How long could she take it?

But I must have misunderstood her, for once again, maman defied all odds and survived. Once more, she made it back to us. Fate threw all the turd it could find at maman and she still chose to return to us, which was why I always believed she would come back to us, no matter what. That nothing could bring maman down, and we had a lot of time in our hands.
She was still to see me and Jawad get married after all.

So when I held her warm hands with my own and felt her delicate skin against mine, I did not know it would be the last time they’d ever be this warm. That the ever-aging hands of maman would suddenly turn ice cold, and hard as stone only seven hours after that.
And the funniest part, this is me only guessing. I do not know whether she really is cold and hard as I say, for I still haven’t touched a part of her. It is only what I’m told dead people feel like.

My aunts made their way one by one, gently pried the kafan from her face to expose it and laid gentle kisses on her forehead in a silent farewell. I knew they were crying, I could hear them in the silence, but any noise louder than that and things could get ugly.

The people poured in like rushing water, some even coming to pat us on our heads and offer chaste kisses on our cheeks, but I was too out of it to address them. They didn’t mind. I was bereaved after all.

My sisters were now starting to talk, deciding on which guests to greet, and when it would be our turn to bid farewell. Some of our closest female cousins were huddled around them, offering support when it came to greeting the more unfamiliar faces. My sisters were handling it fairly better than me. Why?
Was it because they already had families after marrying? Another mother to always turn to? Children to look forward to? A husband to lean on?
Then what of me? Who do I turn to?
The only family I have is this. The only mother I had was maman. So, who will I go crying to?
I’m not even married yet. Maman never got to see me marry. Why…

Baba and Jawad made their way inside the room, and instantly the hubbub disappeared. It was only then did I finally lift my head up and look at them, at anyone at all. My face, veiled under the niqab, was evidently bone dry, unlike my sisters.  I was still to shed a single tear.
Baba’s face was moist just like the rest of them, eyes bloodshot as he fidgeted with his cuffs before turning to all his daughters.
“Waqt ast.”
It is time.
Color of Death

The bile stuck in my throat suddenly felt like it was turning to lead, making it harder for me to swallow as my sisters all got to their feet at once, expecting me to do the same. Like the puppet I was, I did, albeit in shaky legs, for I knew what was to come next. I had seen what happened next in kaka Ibrahim's funeral.

The first to break down in a fit of tears was Marzia herself, for she had always been the louder one among all when it came to crying. Hamid had rushed to her in an attempt to lower her voice so the elderly wouldn’t frown at her, making Farid rush to Soraya too although his wife was much quieter than Marzia. Cousin Bushra held Laila as she cried her heart out, her niqab sticking to her face as she glanced at maman before burying her face in Bushra’s shoulder. Jawad stood beside Nilab and patted her on the shoulder with one hand in order to calm her whimpers while also wiping his own tears on the side.
They were all expressing their grief at the loss of their mother. It was the most normal thing to do. So why was I yet to shed a tear?
“Roya.” I heard maman’s voice in my head, the last time she ever called my name as she gently grabbed my hands in her soft warm ones, smiling at me as her eyes turned to crescents. “
Biya pesh az in-ke meyla basta shawa, yak bar-e diga berem, janam?
(Let’s go to the fair once more before it closes, alright?)”

I grin plastered on my face, her suggestion making me giddy all over knowing how against she was about going to the fair before until we had forced her to come. For the first time in years, maman had seen the outside world without the hospital windows and it’s safe to say, she loved it. I eagerly nodded, placing my hands on top of hers. “
Chera ke na? Waqti Soraya bargasht, yak bar-e diga merem.
I don’t see why not? Let us go again when Soraya returns.)”
Bale! Bale, hatman merawim!
(Yes! Yes, we will!)
” Maman agreed like a child. “
Wa in bar metanem Jawad ra ham ba khod bebarim, Farzana ra ham. Motma'en hastam ke u ham khosh meshawa ba Jawad yakja biyaya.
And we can also take Jawad with us this time, and Farzana as well. I’m sure she’d love to come along with Jawad.)”

My smile faltered at the name, but I held my ground and agreed, despite knowing all too well that the woman named Farzana would never join. For she was not even real to begin with. She was someone maman had created in her own mind.
Have I mentioned that maman’s memory has been failing more and more lately due to dementia? Oftentimes, it was hard for her to even recognize us.
Albata.
Of course.)” I forced my smile to stay. “
Farzāna ham bā mā meyāya.
Farzana will come along too.)”
Someone must have pulled maman’s hand out of the kafan, because now it was out on display, and that was the first thing I noticed the moment I decided to look up.
Maman’s hand, once a warm beige, now a pale grey. Like the color of death.
And then, the first drop of tear fell.
The Windows of the Soul

I remember kaka Ibrahim’s funeral. Baba, Jawad, Laila and I were the only ones who could go. Baba was devastated, for it was his oldest brother and the one who adored him the most. Kaka Ibrahim was a kind soul indeed, he was the only one who made this place feel like home since we returned to Afghanistan. Now he was gone, and his home felt like a distant memory of the past.

Laila and I had gone with his daughter’s-in-law to bid him farewell, and behind us was his wife and two sisters. They cried like they had never cried before, howling so loud I feared the men would come barging in. But nobody did. It was Kaka Ibrahim’s family after all.

Laila was crying too, holding on to kaka Ibrahim’s granddaughter as she too bawled her eyes out. I too was crying, but I could not bring myself to be loud, I barely interacted with him. Yes, he was a great man, good to my family, and baba loved him a lot. I spied baba through the door watching Laila and me, and that was what made me tear up, seeing baba cry like a little boy for his brother.
Kaka Ibrahim didn’t look anything like himself.
They say the soul defines most of our appearance, and perhaps it was because the body no longer had a soul, kaka Ibrahim looked unrecognizable.
Maman must look beyond unrecognizable too.
I remember her chubby cheeks, her lopsided smile that I inherited. The way her eyes would crinkle when she chuckled, or how her once stubby hands turned wrinkly not with age, but with illnesses.
Her hands.
They were unrecognizable.

“M-Mam… maman.” The first word of the day had finally slipped my lips, barely audible, but out nonetheless. My sisters were calling out to her more and more, as if begging her to wake up and come back to them, only that she never did. Maman never came back.
She was dead.
My maman… was dead. And I only shed a tear.
Was it because I was still to come to terms with my reality? That maman was indeed gone? Is that why I couldn’t even bring myself to help in washing her body when my sisters did it just fine?
Were they fine?

With trembling lips and eyes burning with unshed tears, I finally willed myself to do that one thing I had not done in the last seven hours. I had not looked at maman’s face even once, even when I had refused to help in washing her body. Too scared of what I would find, or how it would feel to touch her, I ran away, leaving my sisters to complete the task.
I could not bring myself to look at a version of her that will never look back at me again.
But goodbyes only come once, and sometimes don’t come at all. Only the fortunate get to say goodbye. Should I count myself fortunate to get a chance to see my maman’s dead face?

Someone held back a moan, a male, and instantly, my eyes shot up, only to find baba, once again, crying to himself silently, just like the day kaka Ibrahim had died. Only this time he wasn’t a little boy, but a husband that lost his wife.
Baba, the strongest figure I know, cried his heart out as he stared at his wife’s face. Maman’s face.
And as if that was the push I needed, I too did the same.
I did not wait to brace myself, or tell myself I didn’t need to. Before I knew it, I was already looking at her, and oh… I was right.
Maman was unrecognizable.
Gaunt cheeks replaced her chubby ones, mouth slightly parted in a final sigh. hairs pushed back to expose her full face and her eyes, her pretty chocolate brown eyes…
I could not see them. They were hidden behind the veil of death.

“Maman.” I whispered, and all too suddenly, it seemed like the body was coming to life. As if I had just spoken the magic word, and the body on the bier was becoming the maman of my memories. The maman I knew.

“Maman?” Like a fool, or like a child lost, I called out for my mother, eyes stinging with tears as the second drop fell and then the third, while my trembling hands lifted up to hover over her own cold once. Those warm hands that held mine not long ago, making me promise about the fair.
Will they still be that warm?
My fingers closed around her own, and I flinched.
It was ice cold.
Maman was dead. Right before me.
Death’s Embrace

Why did nobody ever tell me that goodbyes were this painful? Is it because it cannot be described in words? Is that why I cannot put into words as to what it feels like holding my mother’s ice-cold hand in mine?

With trembling hands, I lift her hand up to my veiled cheeks, trying to feel anything at all, only to come out empty handed. It’s hard and stiff like cardboard, but the wrinkles say this is maman no doubt.

I want to ask her to wake up like Marzia is doing, howl and cry like madar kalan is doing as she feigns to miss her daughter, but my voice seems to fail me. All I can do is whimper like a lost kitten, hold on to her hand as it gets heavier in mine and repeat one word over and over again.
“Maman. M-maman…”

It’s getting harder to speak with the never ending bile stuck to my throat, and the burning in my eyes as the unshed tears finally spill out, first once, then twice, then thrice, until I lose count. I’m finally crying, finally mourning my mother, and I do not even know what to say.
What should I say? That I miss her? That I wish she was still here? Will she hear me?

All around me is my family tearing their hearts out at the loss before us, the noises so loud one could go deaf, but everything feels like a distant siren to me. Like I’m under water. No one, but just maman and me in our own world.
When holding onto her hand gets exhausting, I reach for her gaunt face, brushing a trembling finger over her concrete like face which makes me sob even harder, knowing how much she’d hate this.
Maman always took care of her skin. She always had a Glow & Lovely cream that she applied, and when Marzia married, she brought her a better Nivea moisturizer. She’d hate her skin like this.
“Oh maman…” I wailed despite myself unable to hold myself back anymore as I buried my face in her chest and let it all out.
What do I do now? How do I live in a world where maman is no more?
She will never see me married, never see my children, never get to travel like we promised her. She had only started enjoying the little joys in life, and now she was gone.
What could I do now!?

“MAMAN!” I felt hands nudging me to let her go, trying to pry me off of her but I could not do so yet. I could not let go. I could not let her be buried under all that soil. Maman still had so much to see. I still had so much time to spend with maman. Why must I lose her so?

“Roya. Roya!” My siblings were hugging me now, in an attempt to pry me off as we cried our hearts together. Someone must have pulled the kafan over maman’s face, because now I no longer could see it, and that sent me in a panic mode.
“Maman! Maman!”

But my cries fell to deaf ears, because soon, the bier was lifted, and baba, Jawad, Hamid, Farid, and the rest of the men took my mother away from her home one last time, to put her to her final resting place. And all I could do was wonder one thing as the sorrow began to settle in.
What will I do if maman ever dies like this?
The Voice in My Head

“M-Maman…” My wails were slowly turning to whimpers the moment the realization dawned on me that the bier was long gone from the room. It was time for me to come back to reality, but oh did it hurt so much.

The idea of me never being able to see maman smile despite all her illnesses again was like the fires of Jahannam for me. Which was all the more reason I should be pulling myself together now. I must.

I tried to compose my breathing, but the tears that began flowing would just not stop. My eyes were still closed in denial, the last scene being that of maman in the bier, resting in her living room one last time.
That image needed to go.
…Wa baʿdesh, ba Jawad megoyam az Farzana beporsa ke u ham mekhaya ba ma biyaya ya na. Ya fekr mekoni khodam azash beporsam? Roya jan?
…and then, I will ask Jawad to ask Farzana if she would like to come too. Or do you think I should ask her myself? Roya?)”
My breathing was still erratic, hands still trembling, but the images before my eyes were now turning into a blur, as if dissolving.
Roya? Roya jan, bacham, chera inqadr gerya mekoni?
Roya? Roya, my child, what has you crying so?)”

As soon as the voice registered itself in my mind, the images of my ancestral home living room were gone, and so was the nauseous scent of incense. The hubbub had died down too, replaced by a sheer sense of peaceful silence, the scent of warm sunlight wafting around me. And the next time I opened my eyes, my surroundings were completely different, but not unfamiliar.
I was home. Back in Kabul.
With maman.

“Roya.” The warmth of her hand in mine began to course through me all over again, as if she was breathing life into me anew. As if I was the one coming back from death. But nobody had died to begin with. Maman was right here, right before me.
Gerya nakon, bachem. Hama-chi jor mesha.
Don’t you cry, my child. It will be alright.)”

A gasp escaped my lips, like someone had pulled me out of water and filled my lungs with air again, realization dawning on me over what I had done. Or what I was doing. Crying my heart out over something I had created on my own, by myself, in my head. A figment of my imagination.
But it felt… so real, maman’s death felt… so inevitable.
What was I thinking?
Hama-chi jor mesha. Dafʿa-ye baʿd ke ba meyla raftem, har chi khasti barat mekharam, ha?
(It will be alright. I shall buy you whatever you ask the next time we go to the fair, hmm?)”
Maman’s aging hands reached out to wipe the tears I had shed over the idea of her eminent end, one that has never even happened yet, but felt so real in my head.

Perhaps, everything will be alright indeed. It will be. The tragedy I imagined just now is nothing but just what I said- imagination. Maman was not going anywhere anytime soon. There won’t be any funeral in the next seven hours. I was just… catastrophizing.
And I cannot even help it.

Maman may be alive, but every day her survival hangs by a thread. Every day is a walk on eggshells, a ticking time bomb as we wait with our breaths caught in our lungs as we wonder and wait for something… anything out of order to happen. Every day is a survival game for us.
Because nobody knows when will be the last day maman smiles at us as she’s doing now.
For this once, I did not want to tell her that Farzana wasn’t real, and that she was all in her head. Not that I didn’t want to, I could not.
I sniffled, pulling my tears back while leaning into her touch with a smile. “
Har tor ke shomā bekhāhin, māmān jān.
As you wish, maman.)”

For even if maman is alive and well now, our minds have already begun preparing us for the worst that we cannot bring ourselves to face. Our minds are catastrophizing in their own way, showing us what it’d feel like if the inevitable comes to pass.
But the real question is, do I even want to prepare myself for it?
Does preparing me for the loss actually protect me from the grief it brings?
THE END
